newsitem.title: UK: Appetite for sweets grows despite health fads.
newsitem.headline: Appetite for sweets grows despite health fads.

text.p: The appetite for sweets in industrialised countries has been growing over recent years, despite the lingering effects of global recession and health fads, according to a report released on Friday.

The consumption of confectioneries increased throughout western Europe and the U.S. from 1991 to 1995, with Japan the only country out of eight industrial nations surveyed to experience a drop in its confectionery market, according to a report by Euromonitor, a market research firm.

"Major players within the confectionery market have capitalised on ongoing consumer health trends by introducing low-fat, low-calorie and low-sugar line extensions of existing products," Euromonitor said in its report "Confectionery: The International Market."

In monetary terms, Italy saw the greatest increase in confectionery sales from 1991 to 195, with a 38.8 percent rise,, followed by a 22.4 percent rise in Spain, an 18.2 percent gain in the UK, a 9.4 percent gain in Germany, and a 9.1 percent gain in France. Sales in Canada rose 5.2 percent and sales in the U.S. rose 5.0 percent.

In Japan, meanwhile, sales fell 7.4 percent, where confectioneries fell victim to recession, natural disaster, discount retailing, heightened competition and price consciousness by consumers, Euromonitor said.
In volume terms, however, sales growth was more modest, rising only two percent in Spain and 1.5 percent in Britain. Japanese sales fell four percent from 1993 to 1995, Euromonitor said.

Germans won the sweet tooth award, consuming an average of 14.7 kilograms of confectioneries each year at a cost of $94, Euromonitor said. Britons spent more money eating almost as many sweets as the Germans, spending $125 for average per capita consumption of 13.9 kilograms.

The Americans ranked third, eating 10.3 kilograms a year, followed by the French at 8.0 kilograms, Canadians at 7.3 kilograms, the Spanish at 4.6 kilograms, the Japanese at 3.2 kilograms, and the Italians at 2.1 kilograms, Euromonitor said.
